    RESEARCH ARTICLE

    Peer effects and human capital accumulation: Time spent in college and productivity in the National Basketball Association

    View article page
    Richard J. Paulsen
    format_quote CITE

    Starting in 2006, the National Basketball Association (NBA) set a minimum age requirement on players declaring for the draft. Consequently, elite high school players typically spend at least 1 year playing college basketball before entering the draft. This paper seeks to test for the impact of years spent in college and peer quality on NBA performance. Additional years in college are found to have an insignificant impact on persistence in the NBA at various points post draft, a positive impact on early career performance, and a negative impact on midcareer performance, while peer quality does not have a significant impact on performance.

Starting in 2006, the National Basketball Association (NBA) set a minimum age
requirement on players declaring for the draft. Consequently, elite high school
players typically spend at least 1 year playing college basketball before entering the
draft. This paper seeks to test for the impact of years spent in college and peer qual-
ity on NBA performance. Additional years in college are found to have an insignifi-
cant impact on persistence in the NBA at various points post draft, a positive impact
on early career performance, and a negative impact on midcareer performance, while
peer quality does not have a significant impact on performance.
1 | I N T RO DU CT I O N
Each year in March and April, typically following play in the National
College Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I men's basketball
tournament, elite men's college basketball players begin to announce
their intentions to enter into the National Basketball Association's
(NBA) draft. Starting with the 2006 draft, the “one-and-done” rule
in the NBA required that players seeking to enter the draft either
had to turn 19 in the calendar year of the draft or be at least 1 year
removed from the high school graduation of the player's graduating
class. While there are a few domestic players who have entered the
NBA's developmental league or played professionally overseas for
the year following college, what this typically means is that top high
school players play at least 1 year in college before leaving for
the NBA.
There are risks and rewards to players deciding to leave college
after 1 year. With regard to rewards, predominantly Black, often low-
income 19-year-olds can find a large monetary payoff to signing a
professional contract with an NBA team. As there is a risk of injury
while playing basketball, the chance to sign an NBA contract may not
be available in the upcoming year. But as players typically improve
with age at the college level, additional years in college could make
the player even more attractive to teams in upcoming seasons, which
comes with financial benefits due to a draft pay scale where pay falls
as the draft position falls. The framework of option theory has been
applied in the literature to this decision, as players must decide
whether and when to exercise the option to declare for the draft
early. Declaring early is often a good decision for players, though an
increasing share of players in recent years have declared for the draft
early and subsequently gone undrafted (Arel & Tomas, 2012, 2019).
Sports commentators commonly suggest an additional benefit to
staying in college rather than entering the NBA: improved develop-
ment for the player. When doing so, these reporters use any number
of examples of players who have succeeded in the NBA while spend-
ing multiple years in college to support their argument. Max
Kellerman, when speaking on ESPN's First Take, is one such reporter
who has been a proponent of the idea that additional years spent in
college benefit the player's development. When discussing Trae
Young's decision to enter the 2018 NBA draft, Max said “Trae Young
is good and promising, and I believe he would get better with develop-
ment in college with players more on his own level, a couple of more
years.” He goes on to present the example of Kyle Kuzma. He says
“Why was Kyle Kuzma so good? Ya think Kyle Kuzma would've been
good if he came out after his freshman year? Not only would the
answer have been no, he would've never developed into this player”
(Lewis, 2018). But what is not mentioned here is that Kyle Kuzma
played additional years in college because he would likely not have
been drafted following his freshman season. Kyle Kuzma averaged
just 3.3 points in 8.1 min per game as a freshman, while Trae Young
averaged 27.4 points per game. Jimmy Butler is another player often
touted as a college success story. But again here, Jimmy Butler did
not leave college until after his junior year because he would not have
been drafted having averaged just 5.6 points per game as a college
freshman.
While members of the media frequently tout the benefits of
spending additional time playing in college, recent works in the

literature have found that players who enter the league at a youn-
ger age and with less college experience generally perform better
(Rodenberg & Kim, 2012; Zestcott et al., 2020). There are three
important but related questions that this work seeks to answer.
First, do players who spend more time in college perform better
in the NBA? Second, how should teams consider college
experience when choosing which players to draft? Third, how
does the quality of peers in college affect subsequent NBA
productivity?
To answer these questions, data were collected on all players
drafted to the NBA between 2006, when the “one-and-done” rule
was implemented, and 2014. Ending the data in 2014 allows for a
sufficient window after leaving college to assess player perfor-
mance in the NBA. One drawback of past works looking at years
of college basketball experience and NBA performance, like
Zestcott et al. (2020), has been insufficient addressing of differ-
ences in innate ability between “one-and-done” players and those
who spend more time in college. In the sample considered in this
paper, “one-and-done” players were drafted significantly earlier in
the draft and had significantly stronger freshman year college per-
formance statistics. To try to better estimate a causal impact of
spending additional years in college on NBA performance, multiple
regressions are run where the draft position, high school recruiting
ranking, and freshman year performance statistics are included as
controls when estimating the impact of college years played on
performance. In simple regressions of college years played on per-
formance, additional years spent in college are found to have a
negative impact on performance. However, the effect of college
years played on early career performance is positive and significant
when controls for ability are added, and this effect becomes insig-
nificant later in the career. These findings would suggest that for a
championship contending team, drafting a player with more college
experience may lead to a more immediate impact, though college
years played does not have a significant impact on performance
over the longer term. Playing in a power conference is not found
to have a significant impact on performance, which suggests that
peer quality in college is not an important determinant of NBA
success.
2 | LITERATU RE
In understanding how playing in college affects NBA performance,
four related literatures will be discussed. First, a small literature
exists which looks to predict player success in the NBA. Second,
related literature exists in Major League Baseball (MLB) that looks
to at how being drafted from college, rather than high school,
affects professional performance. Third, a literature exists that
looks at peer effects in various sport settings. Last, a vast literature
exists on peer effects outside of sports, primarily in schooling,
which looks to understanding how quality of peers affects
outcomes.
2.1 | Determinants of player success in the NBA
A small literature exists which looks to assess the impact of years
played in college on performance in the NBA. Most closely related to
this work is Zestcott et al. (2020). Using data from 1995 to 2016, they
look to assess the impact of years played in college on career offen-
sive statistics, defensive statistics, advanced statistics, and mistakes in
game play. They find a negative relationship between years spent in
college and offensive and defensive performance, using traditional
and advanced metrics, but also find that more time in college leads to
fewer mistakes. A similar work by Rodenberg and Kim (2012) looks at
the impact of age of entry into the NBA on career performance. Using
data from 1989 to 2000, they find that increases in age of entry into
the NBA have a negative impact on minutes per game, player effi-
ciency rating (PER), and All-Star game selections. Both pieces, how-
ever, do not sufficiently address differences in innate ability by years
spent in college. Players drafted following only 1 year in college or
drafted directly out of high school are typically of higher innate ability
and are drafted much earlier in the draft. Zestcott et al. (2020) do not
control for draft order. Though Groothuis et al. (2007) focus primarily
on time spent in college through the lens of the player's decision to
enter the draft early, they do some analysis looking at the impact of
college on NBA performance. While players drafted with limited or no
college experience perform worse in their first NBA seasons, by the
fourth year in the league, these players perform notably better than
those who spent two or more years in college. Supporting regression
analysis looking at the impact of early entry on All-Star status in the
NBA finds that early entry has a positive impact on being on All-Star,
though this effect goes away when controlling for draft order. While
Rodenberg and Kim (2012) and the All-Star analysis of Groothuis
et al. (2007) control for draft order in assessing the impact of college
years on performance, draft order may not sufficiently control for
innate ability as there is heterogeneity across draft classes. Both Kobe
Bryant and LeBron James were drafted out of high school in draft
classes that are touted as among the greatest of all time.
Several authors have also looked at additional factors influencing
NBA draft decision making and NBA productivity. Multiple studies
find that college performance statistics influence draft order and NBA
production (Berri et al., 2011; Coates & Oguntimein, 2010; Moxley &
Towne, 2015). Burdekin and Van (2018) find that playing in the NCAA
following the “one-and-done” rule does not lead to players earning
additional playing time relative to similar players who do not play in
the NCAA. Ichniowski and Preston (2017) find that unexpectedly
strong team and player performance in the NCAA “March Madness”
tournament predicts higher draft order and better NBA performance.
Motomura (2016) finds that teams undervalued international players
in the draft through 2001. Teams then started drafting more interna-
tional players, and first-round international picks then began to
underperform. Berger and Daumann (2021) find that player high
school rankings are an important factor in team draft decisions, but
that such rankings do not predict NBA success when controlling for
college performance.
